newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai under heavy unemployment pressure.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai under heavy unemployment pressure.

text.p: Shanghai is having trouble handling unemployment despite having found jobs for 660,000 workers in the last five years, Mayor Xu Kuangdi was quoted as saying on Monday.
Xu also told a meeting of foreign businessmen that the share of the China domestic market held by the city's manufacturers was falling.
"Even though great efforts have been made to re-employ more laid-off workers, Shanghai is still facing great pressure," Xinhua news agency quoted him as saying.
The mayor gave no unemployment figures, but previous official reports put the unemployment rate in the city at the end of last year at 2.7 percent.
He said most firms in the city were in the light industrial sector, especially textiles, that are shedding jobs. The service sector, the main area for creating new jobs, remained weak.
In recent years, the city's textile industry has shed 200,000 workers while the service sector has added 100,000, he said. Over the past five years, 660,000 workers have found new jobs.
Another critical issue facing the city was its falling share of China's domestic market, Xu said.
From the 1950s to the 1970s, goods produced in Shanghai had accounted for 25 percent of China's domestic market, but the figure has now fallen to six percent, he said.
This shows the economy in other areas of China had developed rapidly and that Shanghai's marketing methods were unable to meet the requirements of market economy, Xu said.

Looking to the future, Xu said that while promoting existing industries, Shanghai would also boost the development of biological engineering, medical, environmental protection, and building materials industries.
It will also invest at least 45 billion yuan ($5.42 billion) in the information industry over the next 15 years, he said.

Between 1996 and 2000, the city will invest at least 1,000 billion yuan in fixed assets. About one-third of that will be in infrastructure projects such as airports, subways, railways, harbours and highways, he said.
